title: Troop Leading Procedure
source: lesson-troop-leading-procedure.pdf (SOAC Subject 3.1 Sample Group Presentation); reviewer-troop-leading-procedure.pdf

questions.stem: Which list contains the eight steps of the Troop Leading Procedure in order?
questions.key: Receive the mission, issue a warning order, make a tentative plan, initiate movement, conduct reconnaissance, complete the plan, issue the order, supervise and refine
distractors: Receive the mission, issue a warning order, make a tentative plan, conduct reconnaissance, initiate movement, complete the plan, issue the order, supervise and refine
Receive the mission, make a tentative plan, issue a warning order, initiate movement, conduct reconnaissance, issue the order, complete the plan, supervise and refine
Receive the mission, issue a warning order, initiate movement, make a tentative plan, conduct reconnaissance, complete the plan, issue the order, supervise and refine
questions.explanation: The eight steps run: receive the mission, issue a warning order, make a tentative plan, initiate movement, conduct reconnaissance, complete the plan, issue the order, and supervise and refine.
why: Initiate movement (Step 4) comes before conduct reconnaissance (Step 5).
The warning order is Step 2, before the tentative plan, and the plan is completed before the order is issued.
The tentative plan (Step 3) is made before movement is initiated (Step 4).

questions.stem: Which of the following defines a warning order in the Troop Leading Procedure?
questions.key: It gives subordinates enough known information to start preparing and tells them when and where to expect the full order
distractors: It presents the integrated plan with the coordinating details subordinates need
It reveals how subordinates understand and plan their responsibilities
It tests how coordinated actions work together before execution
questions.explanation: A warning order passes available mission information and initial preparation tasks early so subordinates can start preparing while the leader keeps planning.
why: That describes the full order issued in Step 7, not the warning order.
That describes a backbrief.
That describes a rehearsal.

questions.stem: It is the technique of working backward from the required ready time to place earlier actions on the timeline.
questions.explanation: The sample timeline is reverse-planned from the time the defense must be prepared, then works back to the warning order and OPORD times.
why: A backbrief is a subordinate's briefing to show understanding of the plan, not a way to build a timeline.
A rehearsal tests coordinated actions; it does not allocate time.
Priorities of work order the defensive tasks, not the planning timeline.

questions.stem: A company has 18 hours until its defense must be prepared. Using the one-third/two-thirds guideline in the sample, how long does the company keep for its own planning and issuing its OPORD?
questions.explanation: One-third of 18 hours is 6 hours for the company; the remaining 12 hours protect subordinate planning and preparation.
why: Nine hours is half the time; the guideline keeps one-third for the company.
Twelve hours is the two-thirds given to subordinates.
Three hours is one-sixth, not the one-third the guideline keeps.

questions.stem: Fifteen minutes after the battalion warning order, a company commander issues a short order that gives the nature of the mission, the time and place of the OPORD, tasks not in SOP and the timeline, so subordinates can start moving and preparing at once. Which TLP step is this?
questions.explanation: The company WARNO carries mission, OPORD time and place, tasks and timeline out fast so subordinates can start at once.
why: Making a tentative plan is the leader's own analysis and COA work, not a message to subordinates.
Initiating movement is an action that the warning order can authorize, not the order itself.
The full OPORD is issued later at the place named in the warning order.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes an implied task?
questions.key: A task that is not stated in the higher order but is inferred as necessary to accomplish the mission
distractors: A task explicitly assigned in the higher order
A restriction on time or action placed by higher headquarters
A routine item already covered by the unit SOP
questions.explanation: Specified tasks come from the higher order; implied tasks are inferred as necessary to carry them out.
why: That is a specified task.
That is a constraint.
The sample warns against listing SOP items as implied tasks.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a paragraph of the five-paragraph OPORD summarized in the sample?
questions.explanation: The summary lists Situation, Mission, Execution, Sustainment, and Command and Signal. Assessment is not one of them.
why: Situation is paragraph 1 of the summarized order.
Execution is paragraph 3 of the summarized order.
Command and Signal is paragraph 5, where the company PACE plan sits.

questions.stem: A company moves to its sector at 1300H, before its OPORD is issued and before its plan is finished, because in the defense time on the ground is everything. Which TLP step is the company carrying out?
questions.explanation: Step 4 does not wait for Step 3 to finish; the sample company moves to its sector early to start priorities of work.
why: Reconnaissance gathers information on identified gaps; the company here is simply moving into position early.
The plan is not yet complete; the company moves before it is finished.
Supervision and refinement follow the order, through backbriefs and rehearsals.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes a backbrief?
questions.key: A check that reveals how subordinates understand and plan their responsibilities
distractors: A test of how coordinated actions work together
A walk of the line to check positions from the enemy's side
A message that gives subordinates advance notice of the mission
questions.explanation: The reviewer separates the backbrief, which shows how subordinates understand their tasks, from the rehearsal, which tests coordination.
why: That describes a rehearsal.
That is a leader's inspection of positions, not a backbrief.
That describes a warning order.

questions.stem: The enemy has already mortared emitters, so a company plans a means for its primary communications that cannot be direction-found. Which means does the sample make primary in the defense?
questions.explanation: The sample PACE plan makes field wire primary, VHF alternate, messengers contingency, and pyro or whistle emergency.
why: VHF radio is the alternate in the sample because emitters can be direction-found.
Messengers are the contingency means in the sample PACE plan.
Pyro and whistle signals are the emergency means.

questions.stem: Which list gives the priorities of work in the order shown in the sample?
questions.key: Security, positions, fields of fire, obstacles, wire, dig
distractors: Security, fields of fire, positions, wire, obstacles, dig
Positions, security, obstacles, fields of fire, dig, wire
Security, obstacles, positions, wire, fields of fire, dig
questions.explanation: The sample builds the defense in the order security, positions, fields of fire, obstacles, wire, dig.
why: Positions come before fields of fire, and obstacles before wire.
Security comes first in the sample order.
Positions and fields of fire come before obstacles.

questions.stem: It is the place where the enemy will be destroyed, which in the defense is usually the engagement area where obstacles and fires mass.
questions.explanation: Slides 3 and 9: the decisive point is where the enemy will be destroyed; in the defense it is usually the engagement area where obstacles and fires mass (EA KAMAO in the sample).
why: A sector of fire is the area a unit assigns for its weapons to cover, not where the enemy is destroyed.
A phase line is a control measure for coordination, not the destruction point.
A battle position is where a friendly element fights from, not where the enemy is destroyed.

questions.stem: In a defense with two avenues of approach, which war-game technique did the sample group use?
questions.explanation: The sample states that avenue-in-depth suits a defense with two avenues.
why: The belt method divides the area into belts across its width.
The box method isolates one critical area.
A sketch note records war-game results; it is not a war-game technique.
